messages.author: 6db62e08ec862130
messages.subject: rebase?
parts:
With respect to GIT usage, I understand why you always merge at the end
of a branch. However, I'm surprise by the frequency of merges between
branches. Why don't you occasionally rebase issue or feature branches on
top of develop HEAD before you merge back to HEAD? With so many merges,
I find it hard to follow development history.

--
Joshua N. Pritikin
Department of Psychology

Charlottesville, VA 22904

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebase?
parts:
Hi Joshua,

I saw you made another comment regarding git history.

What's the value of following development history? Perhaps if we had an actual use case, we'd be more careful.

Right now, we've made it easy on the developers to move forward rather than add another bit of complicated git process to our process. I find walking through pull requests to be sufficient for browsing history, whenever I need to review what's happened. (Of course, that's relying on GitHub functionality, but eh... we're tied to GitHub at this point.)



Daniel

Can you show a history of a project that does all that you suggest? Just so I can see a difference?

I'm assuming the left-most vertical line is the `develop` branch, and if so, this looks fine to me. I guess I've just adopted the distributed nature and I realize people work on things while other things happen. > The more I look at it, this sort of depth is the right history I'd want
> to maintain instead of flattening it out and losing the idea of
> concurrency, but that's just me.

Ah, you may misunderstand which part of history I am complaining about.
I am only complaining about the merges that say,

Merge branch 'develop' of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan into develop

In my opinion, that should be a rebase. It is perfectly reasonable to
have parallel active branches under development and to merge them to
'develop' when they are ready. I am only complaining about merges in the
other direction.

More concretely, when you are getting ready to merge your branch, I
advocate,

git fetch origin
git rebase origin/develop

Instead of

git pull origin

Or, I suppose you could do,

git pull --rebase origin

but I find the 2 step fetch/rebase sequence easier to understand.

> I'll wait for another screenshot to stand behind that last
> statement.

See attached. This is part of the OpenMx history. OpenMx has fewer
active developers than Stan, but the thing to notice here is that when
merges occur, the fanout of branches is usually reduced (see merges
circled in red).

Ben --- do you want to chime in here? I think you're
the one who knows the most about this.

I, for one, am happy to do whatever others think
best. The merge bubbles are mildly annoying, but
I tend not to think of them. I usually use git log
to look at history when doing the release notes.

I believe we discussed some way to mitigate the merge
bubbles way back when we were learning Git and decided
to keep them for reasons I don't remember and didn't
understand at the time. Is it possible to get rid of
them by fast forwarding instead of rebasing and is that
safer?

I believe the danger of rebasing I was remembering was
about rebasing all the commits in a branch so that it
looked like a single commit when merged. I'm also OK doing
that if there's no danger of losing work. Very rarely,
if ever, are intermediate commits on branches worth saving.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebase?
parts:
On Thu, Mar 12, 2015 at 09:55:51AM -0400, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Joshua, quick question: if someone already did a:
> git merge develop
> how would they go about fixing that to look like a git rebase? Is that
> easy to do?

Assuming your working tree is clean ('git status' shows nothing), then
you can do,

git reset --hard HEAD^ # move your branch to the previous commit

The merge should be gone now and you can rebase at your leisure,

git rebase develop # or origin/develop

On Thu, Mar 12, 2015 at 11:30:31AM -0400, Daniel Lee wrote:
> I was not thinking about changing the develop branch. I was thinking
> about a local branch.
>
> Those instructions don't work if you've made multiple commits past a
> merge. I was hoping you had an easy way to fix a local branch.

I don't think there is an "easy" way. Certainly it can be done, but I
wouldn't urge you to go experiment unless you are confident in your GIT
skills. That said, you can rebase against develop even when there are
intervening merge commits. I haven't tried this recently, but I believe
those merges will disappear and may be replaced by empty commits or
commits with change fragments. Any fragments can be cleaned up with
interactive rebase. Various tutorials for interactive rebase are
available online, such as,

http://andreabergia.com/git-rebase-interactive/

However, I will be entirely happy if merges from develop to topical
branches are created less frequently in the future. Changing the past is
often not worth the effort.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebase?
parts:
Rebasing is fine if it's done on branches that haven't been pushed at all.  Once they've been pushed, they're public in a sense and other people can end up relying on their history.  Rebasing at this stage will break that history and require --force to push.  The issue really is that we often push our branches early.  Personally, I think this is good habit, as it backs up the branch.  It is also the most convenient way to share branches across multiple machines.  E.G., I use around three different machines for Stan development sometimes (office, laptop, server, etc).

One solution is to have a separate personal repository where no one can depend on your branch and you can break history at will.  Then, only when you're ready to merge and run testing, do you push the branch to the main Stan repo.  That said, I personally don't think it's worth the trouble for what is inherently a cosmetic issue.

Cheers,
Marcus
